name: Department of Renaming Things
desc: The public-meeting access form names a hall that has been renamed in the spirit of Trump's geographic order. The directions use the old name; the amendments use both. The clerk has taped a photo of the building to her desk. So far, it's the only document nobody has renamed.

choices.label: Read the whole packet over your road snacks

effects.log: You use a supply pack, lose patience, and save the matching instructions. You can now prove which building everyone meant before they began improving its name.

choices.label: Skim the bold print

effects.log: You spare yourselves the full packet and miss two corrections. Confidence comes easily when the confusing details are on the pages you skipped.

choices.label: Split the packet among the crew

effects.log: Everyone reads a share, but the cross-references get muddled. You've assembled the crew's understanding of a form designed to defeat a slightly larger group.

name: The Efficiency Emergency
desc: After a local efficiency drive cut their jobs, former bridge workers are helping residents around the closure. The council has copied Washington's enthusiasm for accomplishment lists. Its board lists salaries eliminated, costs reduced, spending lowered, payroll trimmed, and efficiencies achieved. The workers would have settled for “bridge open.”

choices.label: Donate a supply pack and help carry the barrier signs

effects.log: You haul signs where the workers direct you, wearing yourselves out. Useful work gets done without anyone needing to invent four additional names for it.

choices.label: Photograph the closure and submit a factual report

effects.log: You save the report with the notice and date. The council's five accomplishments now come with a photograph of where the sixth should be.

name: Civic Center Potluck
desc: The potluck sign says TAKE WHAT YOU NEED. Underneath, someone has added YES, YOU. People are discussing the canceled LFPA25 food program while passing stew. A dishwasher still wearing her work apron hands you bowls. Apparently feeding people is easier when nobody has to explain how it benefits shareholders.

choices.label: Stay for stew and pack three road bundles

effects.log: You eat sitting down, with enough for later. For once, a full plate means dinner instead of another task your boss assigned.

choices.label: Take two bundles and thank the organizers

effects.log: You tell them you're taking their story to Washington. They send food along too; they've heard about how long government takes.

choices.label: Give one of your food bundles to the pantry

effects.log: The organizer makes room on the shelf and remembers your crew. Nobody asks for a naming-rights plaque over the beans.

name: Crossing Block Party
desc: A library-support party has formed beside the checkpoint queue after the IMLS reduction order. There's a grill, a microphone, and a box of free books. 'Books, water, somewhere to sit without buying anything,' says a librarian. 'You can see why we're considered a suspicious use of public money.'

choices.label: Add one food bundle and help at the grill

effects.log: You turn burgers while a parent reads aloud nearby. Nobody schedules a team-building exercise. The team builds itself around lunch.

choices.label: Speak about what free library access means to you

effects.log: You describe somewhere you can apply for jobs without first buying a muffin. People in the queue applaud with very specific recognition.

choices.label: Share two bundles of water and cooling supplies

effects.log: The shade fills with damp towels and quieter conversations. A public service has improved everyone's day without once referring to them as customers.

name: Freeway Mural Crew
desc: Under a freshly renamed overpass, artists are painting dishwashers, carers, cleaners and drivers. The official sign thanks a billionaire. The mural includes the woman who cleans his office. The artists invite you to help with the base coat, share useful supplies, or stand with them for a photo.

choices.label: Help with the base coat

effects.log: Your arms ache, but the crew keeps laughing. It's nice to put working people on a wall without a notice explaining why they're being laid off.

choices.label: Share two packs of water and cleanup supplies

effects.log: The artists thank you and finish the work. Your contribution won't get its own overpass, but somebody will actually use it.

choices.label: Join the artists for a photo

effects.log: You stand together beneath the finished faces. The town's essential workers get a picture where nobody has cropped them out of the success story.

name: Mail Drop Pickup
desc: A volunteer brings letters for your trip: worries, encouragement, things people want Washington to hear. One retired federal worker has listed five accomplishments. “Fed the cat” appears twice. Below it she writes, “He doesn't respect my work either, but at least he's qualified to judge the cat part.”

choices.label: Read the letters together and save them

effects.log: You read every page. Everyone in the van feels less alone, and the cat's performance review gets a unanimous vote of no confidence.

choices.label: Record a short thank-you for the volunteer to share

effects.log: You thank people in your own words. The volunteer hands over their donated road pack; apparently your sixth accomplishment is accepting help.

choices.label: Sort urgent letters while sharing your road snacks

effects.log: You work through the pile together. The snacks run low, but naming what people need feels better than counting how productive their suffering has been.

name: Who Gets to Say ‘No Comment’?
desc: A community-radio volunteer offers a free practice session before the protest meeting. She explains that you can say ‘I don’t know’ when you haven’t checked something. After years of customers demanding a manager, this feels dangerous. The cabinet apparently has a different training program.

choices.label: Practice with the published chat in front of you

effects.log: You separate what the chat shows from what you merely suspect. For once, ‘I don’t know’ isn’t followed by a manager.

choices.label: Let willing crewmates try while the rest cheer

effects.log: A crewmate finishes a sentence without apologizing for taking up space. Everyone applauds like somebody just got their deposit back.

name: Pop-up Mutual Aid
desc: A food volunteer flags down the van. Since LFPA25 was canceled, her shopping list has become a fundraising campaign. She offers ten bucks and a road-food bundle for help loading. The people replacing the safety net would appreciate it if the safety net came with handles.

choices.label: Donate two bundles and film their public appeal

effects.log: You share the organizer's appeal and unload the food. Your audience can see exactly where this donation went. It's being stacked behind you.

choices.label: Take the $10 loading job and food bundle

effects.log: Ten dollars, dinner, and a sore back. Someone thanks you by name. Several past employers could have learned a lot in these ten minutes.

choices.label: Give one bundle and share their public wishlist

effects.log: You pass their wishlist to people you know and leave some food. A modest contribution, but at least nobody has to wait for it to trickle down.

name: Mutual Aid Dispatch Center
desc: Delivery drivers on their day off are matching food requests to rides. A printout of the LFPA25 cancellation is pinned beside the rota. The desk runs on borrowed radios, donated snacks, and people who have already done a full workweek. The efficiency experts have not offered to cover Saturday.

choices.label: Deliver two of your food bundles in the van

effects.log: You follow the volunteer's directions and make both drop-offs. One crew, one van, two deliveries. You resist announcing a Department.

choices.label: Give a supply bundle of spare radio batteries

effects.log: The radios stop cutting out, and the crew hears a delivery confirmed. A small public investment produces an alarmingly immediate result.

choices.label: Learn the system and keep their public needs tally

effects.log: A driver explains the rota and gives you the tally for Washington. Actual competence is surprisingly restful when you've been following the news.

name: The Street Formerly Known as the Street
desc: An official renaming has left the neighborhood with three names for one road and deliveries wandering between them. Residents have made their own directions table. A neighbor offers a road pack for help moving its heavy board. “They found money for the unveiling,” she says. “The arrows are apparently our department.”

choices.label: Exchange the residents' public help numbers

effects.log: You check the contacts before saving them. Directions now come from people who know where things are, an embarrassingly high standard for the official map.

choices.label: Move the board and help correct the posted map

effects.log: You earn a supply pack and sore arms. The arrows point toward actual places; nobody even had to hold a ceremony.

choices.label: Thank them and follow their directions

effects.log: They wave you off by the right exit. You enjoy a rare government-adjacent experience that ends with knowing where you're going.

name: Overpass Pop-Up Stage
desc: Under an overpass, a community troupe is putting on a show about the IMLS reduction order. The villain is an unattended spreadsheet. A performer invites you to watch or join the discussion afterward. Their entire lighting budget is the sun, which has so far refused to sponsor a senator.

choices.label: Watch and share the troupe's public stream

effects.log: You pass the performance along with the troupe's permission. People following your trip get a clear explanation and a villain they recognize from work.

choices.label: Join the discussion about life on the road

effects.log: You talk until you're hoarse about free Wi-Fi, public toilets, and places to rest. The applause feels better than another customer-satisfaction score.

name: Forecast: Still Your Problem
desc: A local reporter is collecting stories about working through bad weather. Her example is Sharpiegate: political pressure on forecasters for contradicting the president. A crewmate remembers a boss insisting the roads were fine because the store was already open. Apparently opening hours affect atmospheric conditions.

choices.label: Answer with your saved weather alerts handy

effects.log: You verify the dates as you answer, wearing yourself out. The alerts support your account; the old manager’s optimism remains difficult to cite.

choices.label: Send a short written account from the van

effects.log: You put your aching feet up and send a short account. Today’s workplace accommodation is a passenger seat that reclines almost correctly.

choices.label: Record one careful interview with supporting dates

effects.log: You match the dates to the warnings and keep the recording. The story survives basic questions, which apparently remains an optional presidential feature.

name: An Interview, Between Refills
desc: At a diner, a local reporter asks why your crew is spending their last comfortable dollars driving toward Washington. She checks that everyone is happy to be recorded. Nobody has been accidentally added to this interview, putting it one procedure ahead of the cabinet’s Signal chat.

choices.label: Answer questions with your receipts handy

effects.log: Checking every total wears you out. Your receipts still give a stronger interview than anyone who keeps announcing how affordable everything is.

choices.label: Give a quick mileage total from memory

effects.log: The shorter exchange is a relief, until she checks your mileage claim. Apparently your estimate took the scenic route.

choices.label: Let a willing crewmate talk while you rest

effects.log: You stretch out in the van while a willing crewmate tells their story. Shared leadership includes shared responsibility for saying ‘what the fuck.’

name: College Radio Phonebank
desc: Students are collecting library-support messages after the IMLS reduction order. A host offers eight dollars for a short recorded spot. Between calls she asks why reading gets called elitist, but every minimum-wage application still expects you to understand fourteen pages of terms and conditions.

choices.label: Join the live call-in

effects.log: You explain how libraries help people look for work and get online. The host laughs at your road stories without asking you to work on your brand.

choices.label: Share a snack bundle and practice calls together

effects.log: You help nervous volunteers rehearse the opening and take turns listening. It resembles customer-service training, except everyone is allowed to use a chair.

choices.label: Record the $8 library-support spot

effects.log: You record a few calm lines and collect eight dollars. A whole recording session with nobody demanding more enthusiasm about a product you can't afford.

name: Service Station Handoff
desc: At a union garage, the mechanic points to a parts quote swollen by tariffs. “They say this brings manufacturing home. So far it's brought your old wipers back from the dead.” The shop can use your spares for a basic service, check the wipers, or listen to what the van's been doing.

choices.label: Use your spares for the basic service

effects.log: The mechanics work while you rest your stiff backs. It's the first economic recovery today that involves somebody actually feeling better.

choices.label: Describe the trouble to the apprentices

effects.log: They take your account seriously and write it down. Nobody asks whether you've considered owning a more expensive van.

choices.label: Use a spare set of wipers

effects.log: The mechanic fits them. You can see the road clearly again, which is more than anyone promised about the trade policy.

name: Union Solidarity Blockade
desc: Outside a parts factory, workers are protesting reduced shifts while the company blames tariff uncertainty. Management's bonus schedule remains remarkably certain. A steward spots your Washington signs and waves you over. There's room beside the picket, a box of donated road snacks, and a crew that understands being told to tighten their belts.

choices.label: Ask where your crew can help

effects.log: You take the spots the steward suggests. Your tired crew makes a decent line when somebody finally lets them stand together.

choices.label: Accept a road pack and pass quietly

effects.log: A worker hands you supplies through the window. “Get there,” she says. “Our complaints keep getting lost somewhere above payroll.”

choices.label: Share a pack from your own supplies

effects.log: You add your snacks to the table. For once, everyone contributing to the economy gets to eat something from it.

name: Water Drive Relay
desc: A water table serves delivery drivers coming off a hot route. The volunteer has taped the showerhead headline to an empty bottle: PRESIDENT GETS MORE PRESSURE; DRIVERS ALREADY HAVE PLENTY. She needs water or help moving cases, and offers road supplies for the lifting.

choices.label: Donate two water bundles

effects.log: The drivers thank you and refill their bottles. You have backed a water policy that fits on a folding table and works immediately.

choices.label: Unload cases for two road-supply bundles

effects.log: Your arms ache by the last case. The volunteer hands over your supplies and insists you take a break, a benefit several employers have called impractical.

name: One Socket, Six Phones
desc: At a roadside repair table, a volunteer looks at six charging cables competing for one tired adapter. Replacement prices have climbed with the tariff notices. “You've got the whole economy in there,” he says. “Too many people depending on one cheap thing, and somebody charging extra to replace it.”

choices.label: Use a spare adapter and take a break

effects.log: He checks the replacement while you stretch and rest. The adapter cools down. So do the people who've been negotiating over battery percentages.

choices.label: Unplug everything and continue without charging

effects.log: The socket gets a break. You don't: the passenger spends the ride bent over one dim phone, reading directions aloud.

choices.label: Use two packs of repair supplies and document the fix

effects.log: You provide cables and batteries, then record the volunteer’s checks and the replacement-price notice. Six phones charge without anybody defending the trade policy.

name: Carry This to Washington
desc: At a library meeting, workers ask you to carry their public budget records and approved stories to Washington. Private contact details have been removed. After the Signal scandal, it’s comforting to encounter an American institution that has checked who should see the attachments. This one meets beside the laminator.

choices.label: Use your spare folders to organize the public records

effects.log: Your spare folders become a packet with a source for every claim. The workers’ evidence is now better organized than the government’s excuses.

choices.label: Give them envelopes and folders for their private copies

effects.log: You share supplies so their private copies can stay with them. Nobody needs a clearance level to understand ‘please don’t pass that around.’

choices.label: Check that private details stayed out

effects.log: You flag a missed phone number; its owner covers it before copying. A consent check works, even without a defense budget.

name: The Rally Address Has Entered the Chat
desc: Your crew chat has two rally addresses, three screenshots, and a confident voice note from somebody’s former coworker. After the cabinet’s Signal fiasco, everyone agrees to improve security. So far this means two people have changed the chat icon to a padlock.

choices.label: Check and share the organizer’s dated public notice

effects.log: You confirm the address on the organizer’s page and share the link. The information arrives with a source, a date, and no mysterious cousin.

choices.label: Trace the conflicting screenshots and save the evidence

effects.log: You trace one screenshot to last year’s rally and save the dated originals. Your eyes hurt. The padlock icon receives none of the credit.

choices.label: Forward the whole batch as current rally details

effects.log: Someone follows your ‘confirmed’ directions to last year’s location. You spend the next exchange explaining how several screenshots briefly looked like research.

name: Please Hold While We Check Reality
desc: At a free protest prep session, a volunteer plays a boss denying something you can see with your own eyes. The exercise uses Sharpiegate. Everyone with customer-service experience recognizes the format immediately: the person holding the marker would like to speak to science’s manager.

choices.label: Practice answering from the published investigation

effects.log: You keep returning to what investigators actually found, even as the questions wear you down. Reality requires more unpaid preparation than you had budgeted.

choices.label: Practice one calm answer together in the van

effects.log: You practice saying ‘Let me check that’ without apologizing. It takes three attempts to stop offering the imaginary official a refill.

choices.label: Send your remembered summary and take a nap

effects.log: You sleep beautifully. Later, someone shows where your confident summary contradicts the report you meant to read. Rested, you now correct it.

name: The Public Paper Pile
desc: At a community table, residents have collected public notices about reduced services beside the news of DOGE's billion-to-million correction. Every envelope explains why something they need is disappearing. None explains how to get a billionaire's typing error accepted as proof of income. They ask what you can carry to Washington.

choices.label: Sort the notices by who's affected

effects.log: You save the clearest examples, with dates. It's draining work, but the people reduced to a savings figure have names again.

choices.label: Use your paper and envelopes to send copies

effects.log: You mail copies to the public oversight address and keep the details straight. Accountability still appears to require stationery purchased by the people being cut.

choices.label: Store the files and close the folder

effects.log: You take a breather with the evidence safely saved. For a few minutes, no one has to prove that needing a public service is reasonable.

name: Private Chat, Public Application
desc: At a motel’s odd-job signup table, the manager wants your details in an old staff chat. A housekeeper recognizes former employees and the vending-machine repairman. He says encryption makes it fine. ‘Signal all over again,’ she says. ‘Funny how the time clock always knows exactly who I am.’

choices.label: Check the roster and record the signup problem

effects.log: With her permission, you note the stray contacts without copying private details. At least this mess has an understandable cause and a written record.

choices.label: Take the manager’s word and reassure the crew

effects.log: You repeat the manager’s assurance. Then a former employee replies to the signup thread. Your privacy assessment has failed the ‘who is this’ test.

choices.label: Offer paper and get the access policy in writing

effects.log: The manager writes who can see the form on your paper; the housekeeper confirms where it goes. Paper has won the technology demonstration.

name: The Public Comment Endurance Test
desc: The public hearing has spent an hour congratulating itself for demanding proof that workers do useful things. You're still waiting for the public-comment microphone. A cleaner beside you checks when her next shift starts. Apparently the public is welcome to participate, provided it can arrange to stop being employed.

choices.label: Stay, use your road snacks and give your comment

effects.log: You finally get your account into the record, exhausted and down a supply pack. Three minutes for the public. The self-congratulation had no timer.

choices.label: Withdraw your comment and walk back to the van

effects.log: The long walk aches, but the speeches are finally behind you. Your account stays unheard; the chair gets to congratulate the meeting for finishing efficiently.

choices.label: Step into the hallway for a breather

effects.log: You recover your patience and miss your turn at the microphone. The cleaner nods. She, too, has been marked absent while keeping herself functional.

name: Public Accountability, Folding Chairs
desc: A community center is screening a discussion of political pressure on weather forecasters. The coffee is burnt, the chairs have opinions about your spine, and the officials on-screen explain why nobody was technically responsible. You’ve heard that one whenever payroll loses a shift.

choices.label: Follow along with the published investigation

effects.log: You check the discussion against the findings until your head aches. The documented sequence is much clearer than anyone’s account of who was in charge.

choices.label: Save the recording for a calmer review

effects.log: You bookmark the recording and step outside. Tomorrow you can examine institutional failure without a folding chair contributing its own findings.

choices.label: Pass along the quick recap and go rest

effects.log: Your borrowed recap gets a detail wrong while you sleep in the van. Somebody else supplied the confidence; your name gets the correction.

name: Receipts at the Community Table
desc: At a community meeting, a retired bookkeeper is comparing residents' notices with published savings claims. After DOGE corrected a contract from eight billion to eight million, she started bringing a calculator. “It isn't a political affiliation,” she says, setting it beside the biscuits. “It's a calculator. Apparently that's where we are.”

choices.label: Use your paper to share documented examples

effects.log: You make copies and save the checked notes. The calculator has no billionaire owner to impress, which makes the meeting considerably shorter.

choices.label: Listen and ask where the figures came from

effects.log: People explain what they know and what they don't. Hearing somebody finish a sentence with “we're checking” is unexpectedly soothing.

choices.label: Post the rough notes before they're checked

effects.log: Your summary travels farther than its corrections. The bookkeeper asks you to fix the numbers; you're briefly on the wrong side of the calculator.

name: Fundraiser Detour
desc: A volunteer invites you to a fundraiser replacing canceled food-purchasing support. Guests who can spare them are bringing two food bundles. The largest logo on the sponsor wall belongs to a company that donated the logo. Around it, people who just clocked out are setting up actual food.

choices.label: Bring two bundles and meet the organizers

effects.log: You put food on the table and explain the trip. The organizers remember the crew who contributed something they could open and eat.

choices.label: Thank them and stay on the route

effects.log: The volunteer wishes you a good trip. Nobody makes you justify being broke, which saves you an entire evening of preparing a defense.

name: Corporate Says It’s Healthy
desc: A wellness pop-up offers free raw-milk samples beside a bowl of wrapped snacks. The brand’s MAHA-themed placard promises ‘government-backed science.’ The attendant says the reference sheet came from the office that sent her a uniform in the wrong size. She is not paid enough to defend either.

choices.label: Try the raw-milk sample

effects.log: Your stomach objects, and every mile starts sounding too far from a bathroom. The placard’s confidence has declined to accompany you.

choices.label: Decline and check the brand’s study links

effects.log: The linked paper isn’t about milk. You show the attendant, who thanks you for an answer better than ‘ask corporate.’

choices.label: Take the complimentary wrapped snacks

effects.log: You take the snacks and thank the attendant. They’re going in the van, where the only cleanse anyone requested involves the floor mats.

name: Tariff Whiplash
desc: A parts-exchange clerk is comparing your trade slip with a tariff-revised list. Her shop now wants more of your usable spares to settle the exchange. She has three updates, two corrections, and an email telling her to remain positive. Your supplies haven’t multiplied. Neither has her lunch.

choices.label: Check the terms and hand over two packs of spares

effects.log: You match the dated slips and document the surcharge before handing over your spares. Your careful paperwork proves exactly how much this deal got worse.

choices.label: Insist an extra pack was part of the deal

effects.log: The clerk hands it over, unconvinced. You leave with more supplies and the uncomfortable feeling of passing the uncertainty to another worker.

choices.label: Compare the dated slips and offer one pack of spares

effects.log: The clerk confirms the mismatch and accepts the smaller exchange. You keep the corrected terms; her instruction to stay positive has not been corrected.

name: Has Anyone Tried Paying the Rent?
desc: At a housing meeting, a council member drifts into a wellness speech and waves a MAHA report with disputed citations. A woman asks whether any of its studies cover rent. He tells her health is about choices. Apparently landlords are the only people allowed to make those.

choices.label: Wait your turn and read the posted rent figures

effects.log: After a long, draining wait on your feet, you read the posted figures aloud. The council member abruptly discovers the meeting’s strict time limit.

choices.label: Stay and hear the neighbors out

effects.log: Your legs ache, but nobody has to pretend the problem is personal failure. A landlord’s ‘wellness fee’ gets the room laughing together.

choices.label: Join a quieter group and talk from memory

effects.log: The smaller group is a relief. Then someone checks your claim that rents doubled this year. You withdraw it with considerably less council-member confidence.

name: Heartland Waystation
desc: Food-aid drivers wave you onto a cleared stretch of road. They're comparing routes and the LFPA25 cancellation over a pot of coffee. One points out a way around the backlog. It is the first infrastructure briefing you've attended where the speaker has actually driven on the infrastructure.

choices.label: Help stack empty crates, then take the shortcut

effects.log: You lend a few hands and get the quickest route out. The directions contain landmarks, turns, and no promise to establish a task force.

choices.label: Stay for their coffee, then take the easier route

effects.log: The drivers send you off with warm coffee and a less crowded route. Progress arrives a little slower, with everybody in a better mood.

name: Rust Belt Convoy
desc: Freight drivers are waiting beside loads delayed by changing tariff paperwork. Their dispatcher calls this flexibility; the drivers call it another evening missed at home. One group knows a direct back-road route. The rest will take the marked detour together. Either way, there's room for one ordinary van.

choices.label: Share road snacks and follow the first group

effects.log: You split a supply pack, then follow at a sensible distance. The drivers' directions move you farther than the entire morning's official updates.

choices.label: Join the group on the marked detour

effects.log: You keep your place and leave room for everyone to merge. Turns out a functioning transport policy can begin with not being an asshole.

name: The Flagger Knows the Way
desc: A flagger is directing traffic around a closure beneath a banner celebrating savings. Someone has taped DOGE's billion-to-million correction to its corner. She points out a coned shoulder route and a slower open lane. “Follow my hand,” she says. “The banner's been directing people into a fence all morning.”

choices.label: Take the coned route when she signals

effects.log: You make good progress by listening to the person doing the work. The banner remains available for interviews about its leadership.

choices.label: Wait for the easier merge into the open lane

effects.log: She waves you into a steady flow. You get moving without the whole crew simultaneously explaining how to drive, a substantial public benefit.

name: No Subscription Required
desc: A volunteer medic offers the crew chairs and a basic check after a hot stretch of road. Across the street, a wellness banner promises to ‘take your health back.’ The medic asks if anyone needs water. It’s the first health pitch today that hasn’t tried to sell you your own body.

choices.label: Wave the medics off and keep moving

effects.log: You insist everyone is fine and spend the next stretch worrying about everyone. Apparently refusing help creates its own unpaid administrative position.

choices.label: Sit for the medic’s care and open your water

effects.log: You use water from your supplies while the medic checks you over. Feeling better turns out to require a chair, not a checkout page.

choices.label: Donate bandages and record the station’s supply needs

effects.log: You hand over bandages and copy the medic’s supply tally for Washington. The shortage now has numbers; the wellness banner still has adjectives.

name: Five Accomplishments, One Exhausted Crew
desc: Parked for the night, you try to finish tomorrow's comment about the five-accomplishment demands. Today's crew accomplishments include finding a toilet and not crying in it. A night attendant offers to let you know when the nearby public venue opens. You can keep working, take turns, or accept the help.

choices.label: Keep everyone awake until the notes are finished

effects.log: The notes get longer as everyone's patience gets shorter. At last, you've recreated a workplace meeting without the inconvenience of being paid.

choices.label: Share a supply pack and take turns finishing the notes

effects.log: Food and short shifts let everybody get some rest. The finished comment contains no inspirational claims about the value of running on empty.

choices.label: Accept the attendant's offer and get some sleep

effects.log: You gain a local supporter and a chance to rest. Nobody asks him for five reasons to care about strangers.

name: Emergency Straw Reserve
desc: A roadside shop has built a plastic-straw display for Trump's order. It blocks half the water cooler. The cashier offers ten bucks to count the boxes so she can clear it. 'He signed one order,' she says. 'Mine comes with a lifting requirement.'

choices.label: Buy two water bundles for $6

effects.log: The cashier reaches around the display and gets you the water. Six dollars buys something you need, though it has received considerably less presidential attention.

choices.label: Count the straw stock for $10

effects.log: You count every box, then the manager wants them counted by color. Ten dollars later, you've learned why national priorities rarely improve a shift.

choices.label: Leave the display and keep driving

effects.log: Back in the van, somebody wonders how to get a broke crew declared a threatened drinking utensil. The funding prospects might improve.

name: Five Things Corn Did Last Week
desc: A farm owner liked Washington's five-accomplishment emails enough to make the workers copy them. One worker offers eight dollars from the office budget to put her handwritten notes into the form. Four entries describe keeping the corn alive. The fifth box is empty. The corn has declined to elaborate.

choices.label: Help her document the work the form leaves out

effects.log: You save a copy with her permission. Keeping something alive turns out to involve many tasks, none performed by the person who designed the form.

choices.label: Type up her notes for $8

effects.log: She tells you what happened; you put it in the boxes and collect the pay. For eight dollars, management can enjoy some artisanal bullet points.

choices.label: Pass on the paperwork and leave

effects.log: She goes back to the form. Out the window, the corn continues its suspiciously undocumented activity, while somebody with a salary waits for an email.

name: Locally Grown Funding Gap
desc: At the co-op, a grower has produce and neighbors have empty shopping bags. Since the LFPA25 cancellation, the purchasing money is the only one that can't make it. A volunteer offers twelve dollars to help load a few crates. The vegetables have declined to wait for a better political climate.

choices.label: Contribute two food bundles

effects.log: The co-op organizer saves your number and gives you theirs. Turns out a support network can start with beans and someone answering the phone.

choices.label: Take the $12 crate-loading job

effects.log: The crates reach the loading bay, your back objects, and the co-op pays immediately. Working for someone who notices the work feels dangerously luxurious.

choices.label: Thank them and keep driving

effects.log: You leave with your supplies intact. The crew wonders whether a vegetable would qualify for help if it incorporated in Delaware.

name: The Cow Hasn’t Read It Either
desc: A dairy brand’s roadside stand has a cardboard cow and a MAHA-style promise of rigorous research. Its paid demonstrator knows which cooler holds the snacks, but corporate’s study links keep leading nowhere. The cow has been promoted to answering difficult questions.

choices.label: Check the cited titles and save the broken references

effects.log: You save the broken links and mismatched titles until your eyes hurt. Corporate wrote the claims; the person paid by the hour gets the complaints.

choices.label: Buy $5 of sealed snacks

effects.log: Five dollars gets supplies for the van. The demonstrator brightens at a transaction that does not require explaining what corporate meant by ‘science.’

choices.label: Leave the stand

effects.log: You return to the van without snacks. Everyone had briefly hoped the next stop’s main ingredient would be lunch.

name: Optimism Will Not Dry Your Socks
desc: An event promoter insists the rain warning is ‘outdated negativity.’ His Sharpiegate-inspired fix is a yellow sun sticker over the forecast. A worker quietly points you toward the actual shelter notice. The sticker has excellent morale and no roof.

choices.label: Follow the shelter notice and eat one of your snacks

effects.log: You use a snack from your supplies and recover under an actual roof. The worker has provided more shelter than the entire optimism department.

choices.label: Trust the sign and reassure the crew

effects.log: You enjoy five peaceful minutes before someone opens the real forecast. Your weather service is now rated below looking out the window.

choices.label: Skip the festival and keep driving

effects.log: You drive past the food stalls while rain freckles the glass. The crew shares the same unspoken grief about the fries.

name: Gulf of Parking Lot
desc: Inspired by Trump's renaming order, the rest-stop owner has declared a puddle the Gulf of Premium Parking. He offers seven dollars to repaint the little sign. The attendant is drawing a dry route to the exit. “I asked for drainage,” she says. “He came back with a coastal business strategy.”

choices.label: Repaint the small sign for $7

effects.log: You collect seven dollars for turning a parking problem into a luxury noun. The attendant asks whether she can invoice him for wet socks.

choices.label: Help the attendant mark the dry exit

effects.log: You check the route together and finish the map. Visitors can now reach the road without participating in the owner's waterfront vision.

choices.label: Leave before the parking pitch

effects.log: You pull away from the puddle and its ambitions. Somewhere between “fix the drain” and “charge admission,” the owner's problem became everybody else's.

name: The Minimum Viable Library
desc: After the IMLS reduction order, this library is planning for uncertain funding. A form asks staff to price each free service. Beside story time, the librarian has written 'children learn to read.' The next box requires a dollar amount. She also has nine dollars for help checking a small batch of scanned catalog entries.

choices.label: Give one snack bundle to the reading table

effects.log: The volunteers set out your snacks and remember the crew. Story time begins with something to eat and no invitation to upgrade to a premium childhood.

choices.label: Take the $9 catalog-checking task

effects.log: You check the assigned entries and collect nine dollars. The librarian vouches for your help. So many tiny corrections, all in books somebody actually wrote.

choices.label: Thank the staff and continue the trip

effects.log: You pass the free-computer sign on your way out. Everyone agrees it would be terrible if poor people started finding things out.

name: The Tariff Relabeling Shift
desc: A dispatcher needs a few boxes moved by hand and yesterday's labels matched to today's list. Fourteen dollars for the boxes; two road packs for the paperwork. Nobody asks you to drive a forklift. “The trained operator's busy,” she says. “Moving the same shipment back to where policy wanted it Tuesday.”

choices.label: Move the boxes for $14

effects.log: You earn gas money and sore shoulders. Somewhere, moving the boxes twice counts as growth. Your back would prefer a recession.

choices.label: Match the labels for two road packs

effects.log: You untangle the revisions and collect supplies. By the end, you know which box is which and no longer care what day it is.

choices.label: Pass on the work and head out

effects.log: You leave the dispatcher with the piles. The radio praises American productivity; somebody in the van quietly turns it down.

name: The Patriotic Parts Counter
desc:
The clerk shows you the tariff surcharge on a roadside kit.

“Washington sets it,” she says. “They just put me within yelling distance.”

Behind her, the TV calls the tariffs an economic victory. You check whether you can afford another one.

choices.label: Buy the kit — $12

effects.log: You stow the supplies, then perform the traditional American celebration: checking your balance in the parking lot.

choices.label: Ask for a written quote showing the surcharge

effects.log: She prints one. You tuck it away for Washington. “Make sure they know I didn’t get a raise,” she says.

choices.label: Keep the money and leave the kit

effects.log: The clerk puts it back without making it weird. Neither of you has been invited to the part of the economy that’s booming.

name: The Eight-Billion-Dollar Pothole
desc:
A diner owner offers ten bucks to help haul a few bags of patching mix to the pothole at the entrance.

Inside, the TV replays DOGE’s eight-billion-dollar savings boast. The correction on your phone puts that contract at eight million.

“My offer’s still ten,” she says. “I counted it myself.”

choices.label: Save the claim and the correction

effects.log: You keep both for Washington. A cashier has to explain a missing quarter. Apparently billionaires can be three zeroes wrong and still get called good with money.

choices.label: Take the $10 hauling job

effects.log: You haul the bags while she patches. Ten dollars for the gas fund. Your lower back would like to apply for whatever the billionaire was doing.

choices.label: Pass on the job and drive around the hole

effects.log: Finally, a problem you can solve by moving a little further left.

name: Please Account for the Bridge
desc: A bridge supervisor has borrowed Washington's five-accomplishment idea. The crew's report says which joints they checked, what they repaired, and why the lane reopened. It has been returned for insufficient enthusiasm. One worker points at the traffic. “Would they prefer a live demonstration of what happens when we don't?”

choices.label: Type their account into the required five boxes

effects.log: You use their words, check the details with them, and save the finished report. The bridge now has both structural support and five unnecessary paragraphs.

choices.label: Share your packed lunch while they finish

effects.log: You give up a supply pack and make a friend. The workers get to eat before explaining how much work they've done without a break.

choices.label: Wish them luck and take the reopened lane

effects.log: You cross safely and a little sadly. Behind you, the people who made that possible are still trying to phrase it as an achievement.

name: Reply All, Clock Out
desc: A café owner uses one chat for staff shifts and customer lunch orders. A regular is asking whether ‘unpaid close’ comes with chips. After hearing about the cabinet’s Signal chat, the cashier is unsurprised. ‘Eight bucks to sort these contacts. I get paid to remember allergies, not why my boss added Gary.’

choices.label: Document the mix-up with the cashier’s permission

effects.log: You show the owner which messages reached customers and keep an approved account. Faced with evidence, he discovers two chats are technically possible.

choices.label: Take $8 to sort the contact list

effects.log: Eight dollars and a headache later, everyone is in the right list. The owner calls you a tech genius. You have identified three customers.

choices.label: Decline and head back to the van

effects.log: You pass on the eight-dollar job and return to a van that eats money without offering so much as a shift meal.

name: Hydration Sovereignty
desc: The truck stop's showerhead celebration has soaked its own LIMITED GOVERNMENT banner. The cashier offers nine dollars to help brace the display. Regular showers are free for the promotion if you bring soap. With your crew sharing a van, you've finally found a presidential announcement relevant to everyone's underwear.

choices.label: Use one wash-kit bundle in an ordinary shower

effects.log: You use your soap and emerge feeling human. The water pressure is adequate. For the first time today, adequate is an extremely exciting political position.

choices.label: Help brace the display for $9

effects.log: You hold the stand while the cashier secures it. Your arms ache, but the nine dollars are real. The banner continues to make larger claims.

choices.label: Skip the promotion and keep moving

effects.log: The damp banner flaps behind you. The crew concludes that freedom smells suspiciously like a crew that still needs a shower.

name: The Exhibit of Pending Funds
desc: At a small labor-history museum, an update about the IMLS reduction order sits beside old mill pay envelopes. 'This display shows what workers got,' says the guide. 'We're waiting to learn whether the other one's an exhibit or instructions.' She offers eleven dollars to scan a short stack of exhibit photos.

choices.label: Scan the assigned exhibit photos for $11

effects.log: You finish the scans under the guide's instructions and collect eleven dollars. Even the century-old payroll records have clearer numbers than the funding update.

choices.label: Share a supply bundle and join the volunteer tour

effects.log: The guide shares your snacks and a story about workers who fought for breaks. You enjoy hearing 'people like you' followed by an actual achievement.

choices.label: Thank the guide and get back on the road

effects.log: You leave the museum thinking about the fight for an eight-hour day. The gig-work app on your phone would prefer you didn't.

name: Click Here for Fifteen Dollars
desc: A local editor offers fifteen dollars to test a short list of links in the MAHA report. ‘You don’t have to judge the science,’ she says. ‘Just tell me whether the study on the page matches the study they cited.’ You have performed harder verification to cancel a gym membership.

choices.label: Take the $15 link-checking assignment

effects.log: You log the mismatches and collect fifteen dollars, thoroughly sick of clicking. Washington has outsourced its homework to people trying to buy gas.

choices.label: Vouch for the studies based on their titles

effects.log: You give your confident approval in a cabinet voice, making the crew laugh. The editor opens an unrelated paper. Your actual claim does not hold up.

choices.label: Pass on the assignment

effects.log: Your unpaid mental load is already full, so you leave the paid version behind. The gas fund remains stubbornly unrefilled.

name: The Shelf Is Still Hungry
desc: Federal food money disappeared faster than federal paperwork. After the LFPA25 cancellation, the co-op still has forms for groceries it can no longer afford. A volunteer offers three road bundles for packing, or ten bucks for delivery forms. 'You can pick the backache or the headache,' she says.

choices.label: Pack bags for three road-food bundles

effects.log: Your shoulders ache, but three bundles go into the van. You have successfully converted unpaid federal promises into potatoes, using your spine.

choices.label: Take the $10 delivery-paperwork task

effects.log: You match the addresses and count the bags twice. Ten dollars earned. The spreadsheet still cannot understand why anyone needs to eat tomorrow.

choices.label: Pass and keep moving

effects.log: You wave goodbye to the packing table. Back in the van, everyone is quiet enough to hear the next news alert. Nobody opens it.

name: Manager Approval Required
desc:
A server on break asks where your van is headed.

When you say Washington, she pulls up the story about a journalist accidentally added to the cabinet’s Signal chat about airstrikes.

“I need a manager’s PIN to refund a side of ranch,” she says. “Apparently I have the more sensitive job.”

choices.label: Read the original reporting together

effects.log: You save it for Washington. Being able to back up what you say is exhausting. You see why management is trying to phase it out.

choices.label: Tell the version you remember, with impressions

effects.log: The crew laughs at your cabinet voices. Then you insist a detail is true and can’t find it in the report. You’ve achieved the full briefing experience.

choices.label: Say goodbye and give her back her break

effects.log: You head back to the van. She has two minutes to finish her fries before she’s responsible for the ranch again.

name: The Name Is the Infrastructure
desc: The county has followed the federal renaming example and given a closed bridge an enormous new name. At the visitor desk, six-dollar official maps celebrate the project; a tired clerk is adding the usable detour by hand. The ribbon-cutting photo takes up more space than the road you can actually drive on.

choices.label: Buy the $6 map and check it against the closure notice

effects.log: You compare the map with the posted closure and keep both. Six dollars for proof that the promotional material has got ahead of the actual bridge.

choices.label: Compare the conflicting notices with the clerk

effects.log: Sorting out the contradictions wears you down. You save the notices and the usable route. The bridge’s magnificent new name has not shortened the conversation.

choices.label: Leave the desk and follow the posted detour

effects.log: You return to the van under a huge picture of the bridge. Even the printer got to finish its job before the road crew did.

name: Strategic Straw Inspection
desc: While your van waits at the checkpoint, a drink-stand owner films ‘straw inspections’ to celebrate Trump’s order. He spots your reusable cup and asks you to join the video. His cashier, still waiting for her break, explains that the order concerns federal purchasing. He asks for less fact and more enthusiasm.

choices.label: Share a snack with the cashier and decline the video

effects.log: She accepts the snack and thanks you on camera. His statement about personal freedom now includes footage of somebody being allowed to eat.

choices.label: Read the order and save it with his public claim

effects.log: You back up the cashier and save the text for Washington. Federal purchasing rules, not cup police. Explaining this takes an unreasonable amount of your life.

choices.label: Decline the video and stay with the van

effects.log: You sit through the queue while he starts another take. The crew has now heard more about straws than affordable housing all day.

name: The National Shower Demonstration
desc: A service-plaza booth celebrates Trump's showerhead order. Its 'luxury pressure' is spreading toward the sandwiches. The booth manager offers twelve dollars to help the cleaner mop up. Next door, an ordinary wash costs five. You can now choose between getting wet for money and paying to get wet.

choices.label: Take the $12 cleanup job

effects.log: You finish the puddle, wring out the mop, and collect twelve dollars. Your back has once again been hired to absorb a management decision.

choices.label: Buy a normal wash token for $5

effects.log: Five dollars buys a shower with a door that locks. You spend several restorative minutes without being needed, sold anything, or asked to scan a code.

choices.label: Pass on both and head for the van

effects.log: You leave the cleaner waving for another bucket. The crew recognizes the final stage of every bold new initiative: somebody on an hourly wage mops.

name: The Museum of Very Large Savings
desc: A volunteer-run exhibit has reproduced DOGE's eight-billion-dollar entry beside the corrected eight-million figure. The organizer offers thirteen dollars to check the labels against the printed sources. Next to her sits a quarter in a case marked “One Trillion, Pending Review.” She can't afford a billionaire, but she's hoping you can count.

choices.label: Check the labels against the sources for $13

effects.log: You collect the pay and save your checked notes, thoroughly cross-eyed. Every digit earns its place. The economy may never forgive you.

choices.label: Improvise a tour from memory

effects.log: The crew laughs at your tour. Then you confidently repeat the uncorrected savings figure to a visitor. The organizer has to correct both exhibits.

choices.label: Skip the exhibit and get back on the road

effects.log: You leave the quarter enjoying its promotion. None of you has ever had a performance review go quite that generously.

name: The Ribbon-Cutting Holding Pattern
desc: A transit group has posted the Chicago funding-pause timeline beside a map of hospital shifts and missed connections. They offer nine dollars to help tally rider surveys. 'Everybody says people don't want to work,' a cleaner says. 'Then they argue about whether we deserve a way to get there.'

choices.label: Give one supply bundle to the outreach table

effects.log: The volunteers share your food and swap contact details. It is nice to meet people who hear 'connection' and think about getting somebody home.

choices.label: Tally rider surveys for $9

effects.log: They pay nine dollars and give you the totals for Washington. You keep thinking about the answers: every 'inconvenience' has a shift start time.

choices.label: Thank them and continue the trip

effects.log: You climb back into the van. Six seats have never felt so far short of a transportation policy.

name: Six Dollars for Better Weather
desc: A rally vendor offers six dollars to replace the rain-warning sign with ‘Clear skies ahead.’ He points to a photo of Trump’s altered hurricane map as proof that weather is flexible. You’re fairly sure the flexibility is supposed to be in your schedule.

choices.label: Compare the sign with the forecast and save both

effects.log: You save the official forecast and his replacement sign. Another exhausting little file for Washington, where apparently checking the weather counts as dissent.

choices.label: Take $6 to put up the false sign

effects.log: You pocket six dollars and hang the sign. A worker checks the forecast on their phone; being broke has not made your claim accurate.

choices.label: Turn down the job

effects.log: You turn down the six dollars. Back in the van, you calculate how much integrity costs per gallon and wish it came with points.

name: This Reference Needs a Pulse
desc: A community clinic is replacing a wellness handout after its MAHA references turn out not to support its claims. The receptionist offers twelve dollars to compare old links with the corrected list. In Washington, an error gets a spokesperson. Here, it gets added to someone’s lunch break.

choices.label: Take the $12 reference-checking task

effects.log: You record which links changed and collect twelve dollars, with a headache to match. The receptionist finally gets to eat something while it’s warm.

choices.label: Accept the nurse’s help using supplies from your kit

effects.log: You use your supplies with the nurse’s help and finally rest. No one asks you to select a plan before being treated like a person.

choices.label: Head back to the van

effects.log: You leave the job and the chairs behind. Your health plan returns to the crew asking whether everyone is ‘probably fine.’

name: Patriotic Thesaurus
desc: A coastal grant writer offers paid work translating the same public project into language that will survive Trump’s grant review. The sidewalk is now a freedom corridor. The shade tree is awaiting clearance.

choices.label: Take the translation shift

effects.log: You earn twelve dollars. The project is unchanged; its adjectives have passed inspection.

choices.label: Publish both versions

effects.log: You preserve the original and the patriotic translation. The receipts need no translation.

choices.label: Keep moving

effects.log: The crew leaves the offer behind.

name: High-Speed Replacement Van
desc: After another Trump rail-funding fight, a contractor proposes replacing high-speed rail with vans and motivational language. Their ribbon-cutting team has transportation needs of its own.

choices.label: Deliver their event supplies

effects.log: You collect fifteen dollars. Your van is now the most operational part of the announcement.

choices.label: Document the missing rail money

effects.log: A commuter joins your contacts. The brochure’s dotted line is still not a railway.

choices.label: Keep moving

effects.log: The crew leaves the offer behind.

name: A Building Is Overhead
desc: A mountain-region laboratory is preparing for Trump’s proposed NIH overhead cap. The budget funds the experiment but objects to walls, power and refrigeration. A researcher offers you a practical choice.

choices.label: Take a paid equipment-inventory shift

effects.log: Fourteen dollars earned. You confirm the freezer is an essential scientific instrument, not a lifestyle choice.

choices.label: Share a supply pack

effects.log: The research crew returns the favor with basic care and a new contact.

choices.label: Keep moving

effects.log: The crew leaves the offer behind.

name: Wind Loyalty Hearing
desc: Following Trump’s order against wind and solar subsidies, a roadside energy fair is judging whether the breeze is sufficiently patriotic. A technician needs help that will actually keep equipment working.

choices.label: Help inventory spare parts

effects.log: Ten dollars earned. The wind keeps generating power without completing its loyalty questionnaire.

choices.label: Record the technician’s testimony

effects.log: You gain a contact and an explanation involving actual electricity.

choices.label: Keep moving

effects.log: The crew leaves the offer behind.

name: Desert Shower Freedom
desc: A desert service stop celebrates Trump’s shower-pressure order with a demonstration nobody budgeted water for. The plumber offers to end the ceremony before the tank runs dry.

choices.label: Help shut off the demonstration

effects.log: You leave with water and a working understanding of the off switch.

choices.label: Take the paid plumbing shift

effects.log: Twelve dollars earned. Working under the sink is less comfortable than announcing freedom above it.

choices.label: Keep moving

effects.log: The crew leaves the offer behind.

name: America First, Argentina Next
desc: Trump’s idea to import more Argentine beef has reached a cattle-country loading yard. The ranchers are comparing the America First speeches with the import paperwork. The manifest needs a second pair of eyes.

choices.label: Take the paid manifest shift

effects.log: Sixteen dollars earned. The cattle’s country of origin is clearer than the policy’s.

choices.label: Compare the speeches with the receipts

effects.log: You add the contradiction to your evidence file. Nobody has yet asked the cows to apologize.

choices.label: Keep moving

effects.log: The crew leaves the offer behind.
